subject: math
cluster: Use random sampling to draw inferences about a population
intro: Answer each multiple-choice question about populations, samples, sampling methods, bias, and the validity of inferences. Choose the single best answer.

items.prompt:
A principal wants to know the favorite lunch of all $850$ students at a school. She surveys $50$ students. What is the population in this situation?
A) The $50$ students who were surveyed
B) All $850$ students at the school
C) Only the students who chose a favorite lunch
D) The principal and the cafeteria staff
items.answer: B) All $850$ students at the school

steps: The population is the entire group you want to learn about. Here that is all $850$ students at the school, so B is correct.
A is wrong: the $50$ surveyed students are the sample, the subset actually examined, not the population.
C is wrong: it describes only part of the surveyed group, not the whole group of interest.
D is wrong: the principal and staff are not the group whose lunch preferences are being studied.
solution.answer: B) All $850$ students at the school

items.prompt:
A scientist studies a lake with $4000$ fish. She catches $80$ fish to measure their length. What is the sample?
A) All $4000$ fish in the lake
B) The lake itself
C) The $80$ fish that were caught and measured
D) The length of each fish
items.answer: C) The $80$ fish that were caught and measured

steps: A sample is the subset actually examined. The scientist examined the $80$ caught fish, so C is correct.
A is wrong: all $4000$ fish form the population, the whole group of interest, not the sample.
B is wrong: the lake is the setting, not a subset of fish.
D is wrong: length is the characteristic being measured, not the group of fish that makes up the sample.
solution.answer: C) The $80$ fish that were caught and measured

items.prompt:
Which sampling method gives every member of the population an equal chance of being chosen?
A) Surveying the first $20$ people who walk into a store
B) Asking volunteers to email in their opinions
C) Drawing names from a hat that contains every member's name
D) Surveying only members of the school chess club
items.answer: C) Drawing names from a hat that contains every member's name

steps: A simple random sample gives every member an equal chance of selection. Drawing names from a hat that holds every name does exactly this, so C is correct.
A is wrong: surveying the first people available is a convenience sample, so people who arrive later have no chance of being chosen.
B is wrong: only those who choose to respond are included, which is a voluntary-response sample and not random.
D is wrong: surveying only one club excludes everyone else, so it is not random.
solution.answer: C) Drawing names from a hat that contains every member's name

items.prompt:
A reporter interviews the first $20$ people leaving a movie theater to ask their opinion of the film. How is this sample best described?
A) A simple random sample, because the reporter did not pick favorites
B) A convenience sample, because it includes only people who were easy to reach
C) A systematic sample, because every person was counted
D) A representative sample of all moviegoers in the city
items.answer: B) A convenience sample, because it includes only people who were easy to reach

steps: Choosing whoever is closest or easiest to reach (the first people leaving) is a convenience sample, so B is correct.
A is wrong: not deliberately picking favorites does not make a sample random; people who left later or saw other films had no chance to be chosen.
C is wrong: a systematic sample selects every $k$th member from a list, which is not what happened here.
D is wrong: this group saw only one film at one time, so it does not represent all moviegoers in the city.
solution.answer: B) A convenience sample, because it includes only people who were easy to reach

items.prompt:
To learn how all residents of a city commute to work, a researcher surveys only people waiting at a downtown bus stop. Why is this sample biased?
A) It is not biased, because a bus stop is a public place
B) The sample is too small to tell anything
C) People at a bus stop are more likely to use the bus, so the sample does not represent all commuters
D) The researcher should have surveyed exactly $100$ people
items.answer: C) People at a bus stop are more likely to use the bus, so the sample does not represent all commuters

steps: Surveying only people at a bus stop oversamples bus riders and misses drivers, walkers, and cyclists, so the sample is not representative. C is correct.
A is wrong: being a public place does not remove bias; the location itself favors one type of commuter.
B is wrong: the problem is who is sampled, not how many; a larger biased sample would still be biased.
D is wrong: a fixed sample size does not fix bias caused by where the people were chosen.
solution.answer: C) People at a bus stop are more likely to use the bus, so the sample does not represent all commuters

items.prompt:
A school of $600$ students wants opinions on a new dress code. Which plan gives the most representative sample?
A) Survey only the basketball team
B) Draw $60$ student ID numbers at random from a list of all students
C) Ask students to volunteer their opinions by email
D) Survey the first $60$ students who arrive at school one morning
items.answer: B) Draw $60$ student ID numbers at random from a list of all students

steps: Drawing ID numbers at random from the full list gives every student an equal chance, producing a representative sample. B is correct.
A is wrong: the basketball team is one small subgroup and may not share the views of all students.
C is wrong: email volunteers self-select, so only students with strong opinions tend to respond, which biases the result.
D is wrong: the first students to arrive is a convenience sample that may differ from students who arrive later.
solution.answer: B) Draw $60$ student ID numbers at random from a list of all students

items.prompt:
From a random sample of $40$ of the $500$ books in a library, $10$ are mysteries. A student estimates the number of mystery books in the whole library. Which conclusion is best supported?
A) Exactly $10$ of the $500$ books are mysteries
B) About $125$ of the $500$ books are mysteries, and the estimate is reasonable because the sample was random
C) About $125$ books are mysteries, but the estimate cannot be trusted because $40$ is too few
D) Nothing can be concluded, because only the sampled books were actually checked
items.answer: B) About $125$ of the $500$ books are mysteries, and the estimate is reasonable because the sample was random

steps: Find the sample proportion: $\frac{10}{40} = \frac{1}{4}$.
Scale up to the population: $\frac{1}{4} \times 500 = 125$ books.
Because the sample was random, it is likely representative, so the estimate of about $125$ mystery books is reasonable. B is correct.
A is wrong: $10$ is the count in the sample, not the whole library; the population total is an estimate, not exactly $10$.
C is wrong: a random sample of $40$ supports a valid estimate; size alone does not invalidate a random sample here.
D is wrong: random sampling is exactly what lets us infer about the unsampled books, so a conclusion is possible.
solution.answer: B) About $125$ of the $500$ books are mysteries, and the estimate is reasonable because the sample was random

items.prompt:
A website posts an online poll and $5000$ visitors choose to vote, with $80\%$ saying they support a new city park. The site claims most city residents support the park. Why is this inference NOT valid?
A) It is valid, because $5000$ is a very large sample
B) It is valid, because $80\%$ was calculated correctly
C) The voters chose to respond, so this self-selected sample may not represent all residents, no matter how large it is
D) The percentage should have been rounded to a whole number first
items.answer: C) The voters chose to respond, so this self-selected sample may not represent all residents, no matter how large it is

steps: An online poll uses voluntary response: only people who chose to vote are counted, and they often hold stronger opinions than the general public. This self-selection biases the result, so C is correct.
A is wrong: a large sample does not remove bias; a big self-selected sample is still unrepresentative.
B is wrong: computing $80\%$ correctly does not justify generalizing to all residents when the sample is biased.
D is wrong: rounding has nothing to do with whether the sample represents the population.
solution.answer: C) The voters chose to respond, so this self-selected sample may not represent all residents, no matter how large it is
